AT&T: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

On its third quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 21, 2026, AT&T (NYSE:T) announced that it added more than 1 million subscribers across its high-speed fiber internet and mobile phone services. This milestone demonstrates that combining mobile and home broadband plans helps lower churn, which is the rate at which subscribers cancel service. Three things management said stand out.

1. Network Efficiency Cuts Planned Infrastructure Spending

Building out fiber optic internet, which uses glass strands to transmit data at high speeds, is becoming cheaper per home as construction scales up. Lower capital expenditures, or spending on physical infrastructure, allow the company to protect cash flow while expanding coverage.

We believe this positions us to reach 60 million+ locations with fiber by the end of the decade, with annual capital investment that is roughly $1 billion lower than we previously planned.
-- Pascal Desroches, Chief Financial Officer

2. Bundled Broadband and Mobile Plans Lock In Customers

Combining mobile service with home internet creates converged accounts that are far less likely to switch to competitors. The company's dense metro fiber networks and 5G wireless holdings, which represent fifth-generation mobile technology, create an operational barrier that rivals can't easily match.

In the dense, urban and suburban areas where we deploy both fiber and 5G infrastructure at scale, we believe that our competitors cannot and will not match our operating proficiency, network performance, or exceptional converged value proposition.
-- John Stankey, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer

3. Decommissioning Legacy Infrastructure Drives Cost Savings

Retiring legacy copper wiring reduces unnecessary upkeep costs and streamlines operations across central telephone switching facilities, known as wire centers. Phasing out older technology helps the business move toward its target of $4 billion in annual savings.

Our progress here is picking up momentum, and we now have more than 100 wire centers with no customers supported by legacy services.
-- John Stankey, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer

Looking Ahead

Subscriber growth across wireless and high-speed internet networks continues to fuel operating leverage, which measures how revenue growth translates into operating profit. Management is focusing on pricing discipline, debt reduction, and customer acquisition costs while leveraging structural advantages in fiber footprint and spectrum holdings.

We exited the third quarter with great operating momentum, and we continue to expect full-year Advanced Connectivity service revenue growth of 5%+ and EBITDA growth of 6%+.
-- Pascal Desroches, Chief Financial Officer

AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ: ASTS) sank to a 52-week low of $39.02 on Oct. 20, just 12 days after SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) agreed to acquire Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz low-band spectrum portfolio for $8 billion. Let's see why that announcement torpedoed AST's stock -- and why investors might be overreacting to the news.

Why did SpaceX's move crush AST's stock?

AST SpaceMobile develops low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites for direct-to-cell connections. Its top customers include AT&T (NYSE: T) and Verizon (NYSE: VZ), and its satellites expand their cellular networks to remote areas that their terrestrial towers can't reach.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

AST has launched 13 of its BlueBird satellites so far, but it can't deliver stable cellular connections and generate recurring commercial revenue until it expands that constellation to at least 45 satellites. It expects to reach that target by early 2027, and gradually expand its constellation to 248 satellites over the long term. In addition to AT&T and Verizon, AST is working with dozens of other carriers to reach over 3 billion wireless subscribers worldwide.

In the past, AST and its clients didn't directly compete against SpaceX, which provided first-party satellite internet and broadband services through Starlink. But satellite signals can't penetrate walls and windows very easily, so Starlink relies on mid-band spectrum partners like T-Mobile (NASDAQ: TMUS) to reach those indoor dead zones.

By purchasing Grain's 800 MHz spectrum -- which previously belonged to T-Mobile -- and combining it with a constellation of over 10,000 active satellites (which are smaller than AST's satellite arrays), Starlink can evolve into a fully independent wireless carrier. That could spell trouble for AT&T and Verizon's slower-moving plans with AST SpaceMobile.

Why was that sell-off an overreaction?

It made sense for AT&T and Verizon to get crushed by the news, but AST's decline is less rational. If AT&T, Verizon, and other carriers want to counter Starlink's latest move, they'll need to ramp up their spending on AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird satellites. They could also increase their investments in the company to accelerate those efforts.

Moreover, SpaceX isn't positioning Starlink as a competitor to AST. Instead, it will likely drive more carriers to partner with AST to expand their own satellite networks.

AT&T Inc. T reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of 65 cents per share, up 20.4% year over year, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of 61 cents by 6.56%. Revenues rose 5.3% to $32.32 billion, beating the $31.68 billion consensus by 2.02%.

Growth in fiber and wireless services supported results, with Advanced Connectivity adding a record 769,000 internet connections. The company also added 379,000 postpaid phone subscribers and raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook.

AT&T Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

AT&T Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | AT&T Inc. Quote

T's Advanced Connectivity Revenues Gain Ground

Advanced Connectivity revenues increased 7.2% year over year to $29.48 billion. Service revenues rose 6.1% to $23.9 billion, while equipment revenues climbed 12.2% to $5.58 billion, benefiting from stronger wireless equipment activity.

Wireless service revenues rose 5% to $17.76 billion, supported by retail subscriber growth, converged accounts and pricing actions. Promotional discounts partially offset these gains. Advanced home internet revenues jumped 23.4% to $2.98 billion, reflecting fiber and AT&T Internet Air growth, including contributions from the acquired Lumen mass-market fiber business.

AT&T's Internet Additions Reach a Record

The company added 442,000 fiber and 327,000 fixed wireless internet connections during the quarter. Total consumer and business locations reached with fiber exceeded 39 million, keeping AT&T on track to surpass 40 million by year-end.

The advanced home Internet convergence rate reached 42.8%, representing the proportion of advanced home internet customers also subscribing to AT&T's postpaid wireless service. Its converged customer base expanded by approximately 350,000. Postpaid phone churn was 0.92%, indicating the share of subscribers leaving the service.

T's Business Connectivity Growth Offsets Declines

Business fiber and advanced connectivity revenues grew 8.7% year over year to $1.99 billion, primarily on higher fiber and fixed wireless revenues. This contributed to a 2.5% increase in overall business service revenues.

Business transitional and other revenues fell 14.6% to $1.02 billion as demand for virtual private network and wholesale services declined. Other service revenues were down 8.6% to $148 million, illustrating the continuing shift away from older offerings.

AT&T's Legacy Business Continues to Contract

Legacy segment revenues declined 24.5% year over year to $1.52 billion amid lower demand for copper-based network services. Operating expenses decreased 23.5% to $1.02 billion, reflecting lower personnel costs, network decommissioning and reduced fulfillment cost amortization.

Legacy operating income dropped 26.7% to $498 million, with operating margin falling 90 basis points to 32.8%. More than 90% of wire centers have been approved to stop selling legacy services as the company works toward substantially retiring its copper-based network.

AT&T T.jpg -Shutterstock

AT&T (T) on Wednesday raised its full-year earnings outlook following stronger-than-expected third-quarter results, though its postpaid phone subscriber growth missed projections.

The telecommunications giant now expects 2026 adjusted per-share earnings "in the $2.40 range," higher than its previous guidance of $2.25 to $2.35 and the FactSet-polled consensus of $2.34.

For the September quarter, adjusted EPS rose to $0.65 from $0.54 a year earlier, while Wall Street expected $0.60. Operating revenue grew 5.3% to $32.32 billion, surpassing analysts' expectations for $31.69 billion.

"During the quarter, we added over 1 million advanced connectivity subscribers from fiber, fixed wireless and postpaid phone, our best quarter in more than four years, and our second consecutive quarter with more than 1 million net adds across these services," Chief Executive John Stankey said during an earnings conference call, according to a FactSet transcript.

AT&T added 379,000 net postpaid phone subscribers in what Chief Financial Officer Pascal Desroches described as "a competitive third quarter." That missed the consensus on FactSet for 379,300 additions. The company added 405,000 net subscribers a year earlier and 432,000 in the second quarter.

"We remain focused on adding the right customers on the right plans with the right offers," Desroches told analysts.

The company's shares were down 5.9% in Wednesday trade. The stock has fallen 11% this year.

Revenue in the advanced connectivity segment rose 7.2% to $29.48 billion in the third quarter, with service revenue up 6.1%. Wireless service revenue grew 5%, driven by growth in retail subscribers in underpenetrated categories and converged accounts, as well as pricing actions, AT&T said.

The company added a net 769,000 internet users in the quarter, including 442,000 fiber and 327,000 fixed wireless subscribers.

Last month, UBS Securities said the US broadband market remained highly competitive due to factors including the expanding fiber footprint and increased emphasis on converged telecom bundles. In addition, there is looming satellite competition as Starlink begins deployment of its Version 3 satellites.

Earlier this month, Starlink parent SpaceX agreed to acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio from investment firm Grain Management as it seeks to establish Starlink Mobile as a major US mobile carrier.

AT&T, however, is "the best positioned operator with the largest fiber footprint and upside to estimates as it executes on its convergence strategy," UBS analysts.

Elon Musk-controlled SpaceX swung to third-quarter earnings year on year on Tuesday as revenue surged past Wall Street's expectations, driven by sharp gains in its artificial intelligence and connectivity divisions.

Verizon Communications (VZ) is scheduled to release its third-quarter results on Oct. 26, followed by T-Mobile US (TMUS) on Oct. 28.
